proposals.relationship: Roche credits Foucault’s histories of the clinic and madness with showing links between intellectual changes and practice and unsettling inherited categories.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2016 answer, published2018, pp.160–161. His particular use coexists with his reservation about successive epistemes; it is not adoption of all Foucault’s philosophy. The original books and recording remain unread here.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, DR answer beginning On va commencer, printed160 to161; note8/9.

proposals.relationship: Roche questions whether successive epistemes can adequately connect intellectual change with social and cultural history, while valuing Foucault’s historical work.
proposals.evidence_note: Same own answer distinguishes this reservation from his positive use of the clinic/madness studies and recognizes Foucault’s own awareness of the problem. Particular criticism, not wholesale rejection or independently checked interpretation of every book.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, printed160, opening of DR answer and continuation161.

proposals.relationship: Roche recalls the fascination of Braudel’s material-civilization history and The Mediterranean as resources encountered through reading.
proposals.evidence_note: Own answers160–161 distinguish the1967 material-civilization volume from its1979 reworking. Roche explicitly denies being Braudel’s seminar student; a later presentation of his thesis is different from initial training. Complete Braudel books not read here.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, printed160 first DR answer and161 paragraph beginning Le deuxième.

proposals.relationship: Roche credits Braudel’s global reach but argues that his formation limited access to the historical perspectives of indigenous populations.
proposals.evidence_note: Own first-part answer, printed175, applies the qualification to Braudel and some contemporaries and recognizes exceptions. It is a particular perspective/access criticism, not denial that Braudel wrote world history or a blanket rejection of his work.
primary_locators: First dialogue, Comment embrasser le monde, printed175; DR answer9 in saved numbered answers.

proposals.relationship: Roche credits Labrousse’s contextual political history and advice to avoid another regional or urban monograph in shaping his research choices.
proposals.evidence_note: Own recollection161–163 explicitly identifies him as a pupil and describes the advice. Alphonse Dupront separately accepted supervision of Roche’s self-devised academy thesis. No sole-supervisor claim; political contexts are not reduced to a food-crisis cause.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, DR answers8/11/13, printed161–163, especially thesis advice and revolution courses.

proposals.relationship: Roche identifies Distinction as a repeated resource and credits Bourdieu and Passeron’s account of educational reproduction while qualifying his own use as less mechanical.
proposals.evidence_note: Own answer162 preserves Passeron’s coauthorship and separately names Baudelot and Establet. Political contact and institutional support do not by themselves establish influence. This is specific acknowledged use; complete cited books unread.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, printed162, DR answer10 beginning Il y avait un troisième personnage.

proposals.relationship: Levi uses Roche’s Ménétra as an example of contextual biography, then warns that this approach can make context too fixed for individuals to change it.
proposals.evidence_note: Levi’s own1331 discussion, in Olivier Christin’s French translation, also recognizes rich results and a balance between individual lives and social systems. The subsequent warning concerns an approach exemplified by Roche, Davis and Venturi; it is not a categorical charge against all Roche’s work. Original Ménétra text unread.
primary_locators: Les usages de la biographie, official pageT1_1331, named Roche example and paragraph beginning Cette utilisation; read with1330/1332.

proposals.relationship: Roche praises The Foul and the Fragrant but questions whether its treatment of smells gives enough attention to social differentiation and changing relations between groups.
proposals.evidence_note: Own first-part answer3, printed172, explicitly calls Le Miasme et la Jonquille a very good book before the reservation. This is a narrow methodological disagreement, not rejection of sensory history; the original book remains unread here.
primary_locators: First dialogue, DR answer3 beginning Oui, la manière, printed172.

proposals.relationship: Roche identifies The Birth of a Consumer Society by McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb as a stimulus for his later consumption research.
proposals.evidence_note: Own answer27, printed182, credits all three authors and distinguishes his1981 Le Peuple de Paris from the1982 book. The later stimulus is not projected backward into that earlier work. Archival parallels do not prove direct collaboration; he separately recalls only one meeting with Brewer. Original volume unread.
primary_locators: First dialogue, DR answer27 beginning Il y a un autre déclencheur, printed182 and note23.

proposals.relationship: Roche recalls contributing his study of booksellers’ classifications to Furet’s book-history inquiry and receiving Furet’s acknowledgment for it.
proposals.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer15, printed164, specifically identifies Livre et Société and note16 in Furet’s text. The original Furet acknowledgment was not independently read here. This is a recalled research contribution, not an inference from knowing Furet or sole authorship of the inquiry.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, DR answer15, printed164, ending Furet me remercie.

proposals.relationship: Roche and Vovelle’s jointly organized colloquia provide a teaching comparison of their exchanges over social history and methods.
proposals.evidence_note: Roche’s own answer14 names both organizers and distinguishes1965/1967 meetings from1967/1973 publications. Undirected editorial comparison, not causal priority or identical methods. The complete proceedings and every participant’s argument remain unread.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, DR answer14 on organized colloquia, printed163–164, note20.

proposals.relationship: Roche recalls admiring Le Goff’s course on merchants and his published work while distinguishing that resource from membership in Le Goff’s student circle.
proposals.evidence_note: Own answer20, printed167–168, explicitly says he attended the École normale course but did not enter the EHESS student circle. The later career conversation is a different episode; neither sole supervision nor a complete-book reading is asserted.
primary_locators: Second dialogue, DR answer20 beginning En ce qui concerne Le Goff, printed167–168 and note24.
